title: Adevinta: From Schibsted's Copy-Paste Model to a Portfolio Platform
basis: Reconstructed on 2026-11-12 from the published index.md (paragraph for paragraph, in its own order) and spec.md (accepted 2026-10-21), which it replaces. Intent outcome, the four acceptance criteria, the thesis and the role are copied unchanged from the case-adevinta entry in journal-spec.json. A roadmap paragraph (p03) and a conclusion section (p62, p63; p63 is the published closing paragraph moved under its own heading) were added.

know: Adevinta's five dated phases: the Schibsted federation; selective centralization under the 2019 rule (centralize where 'investment requirements are large and the technology is uniform'); absorbing eBay Classifieds (2021–2023); verticals and the 2023 convergence decision; decentralization and break-up (mid-2024 to 2026).

The layer map of what was shared when, the documented wins (a voluntary Kubernetes platform grown from about 1,500 to more than 4,000 developers, ten experimentation tools reduced to one, shared OCR and media services) and where the public evidence stops (product layers, the fate of the leboncoin–Kleinanzeigen convergence and of SCHIP).
believe: Deciding what to share by layer held up; converging product platforms is a separate investment with its own scope and stage gates.
When ownership can change, separability is a design requirement reviewed like security.
can_do: Apply the two-part test (large investment, uniform technology) to a proposal for a new shared capability.
Ask of each shared capability what a departing tenant takes, what is switched off and what runs twice meanwhile.

audience.who: Chief and enterprise architects of marketplace groups, platform-engineering leads and engineering directors deciding what to share across marketplaces after acquisitions, or preparing for a possible divestment.
already_knows: What an API, a database, an event stream, a search engine and Kubernetes are.
How to make and defend an architecture decision.
Part IX's evidence rules and its first lesson, from part-9.
Global components, tenancy and consolidation sequencing, from multi-country-platforms and platform-consolidation.
does_not_know: Adevinta's corporate history and its brands.
Adevinta-internal names: SCHIP, FIAAS, Houston, Fisher, YAMS, EU5.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a group's proposal to share several capabilities and converge two product platforms, the reader sorts the proposal by layer using Adevinta's dated record and says what the convergence needs before it is funded.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A group proposes to share its cloud platform, its experimentation tool, an image-recognition service and, in a second stage, to merge its two largest generalist marketplaces onto one product platform. Its owner is a private-equity fund. Using only this chapter: which parts does Adevinta's record support, what does it say about the merger, and what must every shared part be able to do?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The cloud platform, experimentation and narrow ML service pass the 2019 test (large investment, uniform technology) and match Adevinta's documented wins, grown by voluntary adoption. The merger matches the 2023 decision to make leboncoin and Kleinanzeigen 'a unified global platform', last reported 'progressing well' in May 2024 and followed by the 2025 decentralization; it needs its own investment case with scope, stage gates and exit criteria. Every shared capability must be tenant-separable (account boundary per tenant, tenant-scoped data with contracts, portable deployment, clear code ownership), because under private-equity ownership Adevinta localized intellectual property and sold Spain as a carve-out.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the opening alone (the callouts and the paragraphs before the first heading) can predict the chapter's questions, its evidence and where it ends.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the callouts and the paragraphs before the first heading: what questions will this chapter ask, what kind of evidence will it use, and how will it end?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Three questions asked of each phase (what was shared, at which layer, what the sharing cost when the strategy changed); evidence from Adevinta's annual and strategic reports, releases and tech blog, strongest on infrastructure, data and organization and weakest on core product layers; an argument for sharing the uniform, expensive layers first, treating product convergence as a separate decision and designing every shared layer so a tenant can leave; a final comparison with Veldmark.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reverse outline of the chapter, written without the spec, lists the same controlling ideas in the same order as the post spec's sections and paragraphs.

Every statement about Adevinta's internal systems that no cited source documents sits in a callout or figure caption labeled as inference, and every company fact outside those labels carries its source and publication year.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Is there any sentence outside an `INFERENCE, NOT DOCUMENTED` callout or a labeled figure caption that describes how Adevinta builds or runs a system without a dated source, or a company fact with no source and year?
acceptance_criteria.expected: None. Undocumented internals appear only in labeled inference callouts or captions; each company fact names its source and year in the sentence or the timeline; the author's interpretation is marked 'my reading' or sits in the Chief Architect's view.

thesis.question: What did Adevinta share across its marketplaces in each phase from the 2019 demerger to the 2025–2026 break-up, at which layer, and what did the sharing cost when its capital strategy changed?
thesis.claim: Adevinta's record supports deciding what to share by layer: its 2019 test, centralize where 'investment requirements are large and the technology is uniform', put infrastructure, data, experimentation and narrow machine-learning services on shared platforms that grew by voluntary adoption, whereas its 2023 decision to turn the leboncoin and Kleinanzeigen platforms into 'a unified global platform' was last reported 'progressing well' in May 2024 and then overtaken by the 2025 move to standalone marketplaces, in which central functions were ramped down, intellectual property was localized and central and local services ran in parallel. Since the record never reports the convergence completed or its savings realized, product-platform convergence needs its own investment case with scope and stage gates; and since a change of owner forced that unwinding, every shared capability must be designed to be separable.
thesis.disputed_by: The reading that Adevinta's 2025 reversal shows central platforms were a mistake and a group should keep its marketplaces independent; or the opposite reading that the convergence was sound and only the new owners interrupted it, so a group should still aim at one product platform for its generalist marketplaces.
thesis.so_what: A Chief Architect writes the two-part test into the group's architecture principles and makes every proposal for a shared capability answer both halves; measures a platform by how many tenants choose it and funds migration engineers rather than deadlines; requires any product-platform convergence to state its capabilities, markets, stage gates and exit criteria before it is staffed; and reviews every shared capability for separability (one account boundary per tenant, tenant-scoped data with contracts, deployment that runs outside the platform, clear ownership of code and models).
thesis.how_why: Demerged from Schibsted in April 2019 as a federation of locally built sites, Adevinta adopted a 'centralised strategy to data and analytics' while keeping product autonomy; its Common Platform served about 1,500 engineers in January 2020 and, as SCHIP, more than 4,000 developers in June 2023, with no mandate in the record. It bought eBay Classifieds Group in June 2021, targeting €130–165 million of run-rate cost synergies, and moved most EU5 platforms to AWS in 2023. The convergence decision came the same year; the take-private settled in May 2024; from July 2024 a new operating model 'empowering local marketplaces' ramped down central functions, localized intellectual property and ran central and local services in parallel, and Adevinta Spain was sold to EQT (announced July 2025, completed February 2026). The case is strongest on infrastructure and weakest exactly where the convergence bet was placed, so its completion cannot be judged from the public record.

supporting_claims.claim: Adevinta's 2019 rule, centralize where 'investment requirements are large and the technology is uniform', put infrastructure, data, experimentation and narrow machine-learning services on shared platforms that grew by voluntary adoption and harvested local inventions; these are the record's documented wins.

The 2023 decision to turn the leboncoin and Kleinanzeigen platforms into 'a unified global platform' was last reported 'progressing well' in May 2024 and then overtaken by the 2025 move to standalone marketplaces, so product-platform convergence needs its own investment case with scope and stage gates.

Under private-equity ownership from 2024, the 2025 move to standalone marketplaces ramped down central functions, localized intellectual property and ran central and local services in parallel: a change of owner forced the unwinding of shared platforms.

Because a change of owner forced that unwinding, every shared capability must be designed to be separable: one account boundary per tenant, tenant-scoped data with contracts, portable deployment, clear code ownership.

The record is strongest on infrastructure, data and organization and weakest at the product layer, where the convergence bet was placed: it never reports the convergence completed or its savings realized.

role.contribution: The fullest public test of the centralization pendulum: what sharing by layer delivered, what product convergence left unproven, and what a change of owner made shared platforms cost.

additional_patterns.applies_to: layer-map to evidence-stops: cross-phase views (by layer, by inferred architecture, by option, by vertical, by risk, by gap)
chief-architect to questions: rules from the record, their test against the book and Veldmark, and questions for the reader's group

flow.rationale: Reading rules and the timeline come first because every later sentence is a dated fact, a reading or an inference. The five phases run in time order because the case's teaching value is the movement of the shared/local line over time (decision of 2026-10-19); read out of order, the 2025 reversal would have no convergence to reverse. The cross-phase views come only after all five phases, because each one (the layer map, the trade-offs, the verticals) uses facts from every phase; the evidence limits close that group so the rules that follow do not outrun them. The author's rules, the comparison and the questions come last because they apply what the record has shown.

hook.content: Adevinta changed its platform strategy several times in seven years, in public: demerged from Schibsted in 2019 as a federation of locally built sites, it bought eBay Classifieds Group in 2021, announced in 2023 that two of its largest generalist platforms would become one, and from mid-2024, under new private-equity owners, ramped down central functions, moved capabilities and intellectual property to the marketplaces and sold businesses.

bridge.from_reader_world: A Chief Architect deciding what a group of marketplaces should share, under owners who may buy or sell them.
bridge.to_topic: One group ran the whole centralization pendulum and wrote much of it down, so each phase can be asked what was shared, at which layer and what the sharing cost when the strategy changed.

thesis_statement.text: Share the uniform, expensive layers first, treat product-platform convergence as a separate decision, and design every shared layer so a tenant can leave.
thesis_statement.placement: KEY POINTS callout (all three bullets) and paragraph p02.

roadmap.placement: Paragraph p03, after the three questions.

promises.promise: Set the reading rules and the limits of the evidence.
Follow the five phases in order, from the Schibsted federation to the break-up.
Look across the phases: a layer map, a labeled reference architecture, the trade-offs, the verticals, the failure modes and where the evidence stops.
End with the author's decision rules, a comparison with the book's patterns and with Veldmark, and questions to ask.

evidence.shows: Shows the full swing the chapter reads.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The chapter asks three questions of each phase, what was shared, at which layer and what the sharing cost when the strategy changed, and argues for sharing the uniform layers first, treating product convergence separately and designing every shared layer so a tenant can leave.

transition_in.introduces: The questions asked of it and the argument it supports.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The evidence, Adevinta's reports, releases and engineering blog, is strongest on infrastructure, data and organization and weakest on core product layers, and the chapter reads it through reading rules and a timeline, the five phases, views across them, and the author's rules, a comparison with Veldmark and questions.

sections.heading: Phase 1: The Schibsted Federation (Before 2019)
sections.controlling_idea: The Schibsted era left a federation of national sites, documented as a portfolio but not as a build, whose most durable shared abstraction was a local invention.

advances_thesis.how: Shows the starting point the later sharing worked from and where the record is lore.

transition_in.introduces: The phase before the demerger.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The public record documents the Schibsted-era portfolio of national generalist sites but not how it was built; the shared Blocket-derived code base is widely repeated but unverified, so it stays lore.

evidence.what: leboncoin (launched 2006), Subito, InfoJobs, Segundamano; the 2012 Nieman Lab '28 countries on the Blocket platform' could not be retrieved.
evidence.shows: Shows what is documented and what is only repeated.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: My reading is that a copied starting code base is the classic origin of the Copy-Paste Country, and that the later phases tried to recover the economics copying gave away without losing local autonomy.

transition_in.carries_over: A shared starting code base evolved locally.
transition_in.introduces: What such an origin leads to.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Adevinta's most durable shared abstraction, FIAAS, was a local invention at FINN.no, a Schibsted site, promoted to group level once it was open-sourced in the year of the demerger.

evidence.what: FINN's 2017 KubeCon talk: about 350 microservices, 1,200 deployments a week, about 147 lines of Kubernetes configuration replaced by a short file; open-sourced 2019; a 2023 Adevinta post still calls it the 'Golden Path'; FINN.no stayed with Schibsted.
evidence.source: FINN.no, KubeCon EU 2017; Adevinta Tech Blog 2023
evidence.shows: Shows sharing that started as a local tool and was adopted, not imposed.

transition_in.carries_over: Copying as the origin of duplication.
transition_in.introduces: A shared abstraction that came from one site and spread.

flow.rationale: What is documented about the federation, the author's reading of the copied code base, then FIAAS, the local invention that outlived the era and leads into Phase 2's platform. FIAAS last lets the next section pick it up.

sections.heading: Phase 2: Selective Centralization (2019–2020)
sections.controlling_idea: In 2019 Adevinta centralized only where investment was large and technology uniform, and its platform grew under that rule by voluntary adoption.

advances_thesis.how: States the two-part test and the first documented win under it.

flow.rationale: The rule as stated, the money behind it, the author's reading of it, then the platform built under it, how it was offered and how it grew. The reading needs the quotation; the growth needs the design choices that explain it.

transition_in.introduces: The first choices of the listed company.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Adevinta's first annual report, for 2019, centralized data and analytics because there 'investment requirements are large and the technology is uniform', while keeping local autonomy in product and technology.

evidence.what: "...we are adopting a centralised strategy to data and analytics. This one area where investment requirements are large and the technology is uniform..."
evidence.shows: States the rule in the company's own words.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The same report backed the rule with centrally developed 'scalable components' and central losses, for a group whose €680 million of 2019 revenue came mostly from France and Spain.

evidence.what: 2019 revenue €680 million: France €357 million, Spain €182 million, Brazil equity-accounted, 'Global Markets'.
evidence.shows: Shows the size and concentration of the group the rule applied to; the prose says so after the figures.

transition_in.introduces: The investment and the revenue it applied to.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: I read this as the strongest decision rule in the record, because it names two conditions, large investment and uniform technology, and accepts that product surfaces fail them.

evidence.what: Figure 2: the 2019 rule as a two-stage test.
evidence.shows: Shows why product surfaces stayed local.

transition_in.carries_over: The rule as the report stated it.
transition_in.introduces: Why it is the record's strongest decision rule.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The Common Platform, written up in January 2020, was a platform-as-a-service for about 1,500 engineers in about 20 marketplaces built from ordinary tools.

evidence.what: Spinnaker, FIAAS, self-run Kubernetes on EC2, Prometheus.
evidence.shows: Shows the platform's ordinary building blocks.

transition_in.carries_over: The rule for what to centralize.
transition_in.introduces: The platform built under it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Its design choices were less ordinary: voluntary adoption, ten-minute onboarding, embedded engineers for large migrations and a bridge that moved services without code changes.

evidence.what: "You prefer to do the plumbing yourself? It's your call, we respect that."; about 200 Spanish microservices; Eurek8s.
evidence.shows: Shows a platform that made adoption cheap rather than compulsory.

transition_in.introduces: The unusual way it was offered.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The platform grew from about 1,500 to more than 4,000 developers as SCHIP by June 2023 with no documented mandate, the clearest counter-example to the Forced Fit in the book's research.

evidence.what: SCHIP, a multi-tenant Kubernetes distribution, 'more than 4,000 developers' and about 5,000 applications (June 2023).
evidence.shows: Shows voluntary adoption scaling through the eCG integration.

transition_in.introduces: The growth it produced, flagged as a look-ahead past this phase to June 2023 and the eCG integration of Phase 3.

sections.heading: Phase 3: Absorbing eBay Classifieds (2021–2023)
sections.controlling_idea: Absorbing eBay Classifieds doubled the group and its stacks, and the consolidation the record documents sits at the uniform layers, with one product component.

advances_thesis.how: Shows what sharing by layer consolidated after the acquisition, and what it left unknown.

additional_patterns.applies_to: p20-p25: consolidation layer by layer (infrastructure, data, overarching components with the dispute back office beside its table row, then experimentation and machine learning)

flow.rationale: The deal, what was removed from it and what it cost come first because they set the scope; the layers then follow the blog's four layers, with the dispute back office directly after the shared-services table that lists it (round-3 readers both read the later position as a jump backwards), and experimentation and machine learning last as the two consolidations documented end to end. The ML Golden Path (August 2024) sits here although it postdates the phase, because it completes the same consolidate-and-harvest path; its date is in the paragraph.

transition_in.carries_over: A platform that grew without a mandate.
transition_in.introduces: The acquisition that doubled the group it served.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The eBay Classifieds Group acquisition, completed on 25 June 2021, roughly doubled the group and targeted run-rate cost synergies of €130–165 million, with every acquired brand on its own stack.

evidence.what: #1 positions in 16 countries, about three billion monthly visits, pro forma 2019 revenue about €1.6 billion; mobile.de, eBay Kleinanzeigen, Marktplaats, 2dehands/2ememain, Kijiji, Gumtree, Automobile.it.
evidence.shows: Shows the scale and the number of stacks the integration faced.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Regulators and strategy removed part of the integration scope before integration began, so the scope is not known at signing.

evidence.what: CMA-required sales of Shpock and Gumtree UK with Motors.co.uk (2021); Denmark to Schibsted; 2022 sales of Australia, South Africa, Mexico; 2023 exit from Hungary; focus on 'five core European markets'.
evidence.shows: Shows overlapping platforms leaving before anyone integrated them.

transition_in.introduces: The parts removed before integration.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The 2023 annual report shows what integration cost, but whether the synergy target was met, and how much came from technology, is not public.

evidence.what: €69 million eCG integration expenses in 2023; €15 million rebrand of eBay Kleinanzeigen; €22 million verticalization.
evidence.shows: Shows the cost side of the synergy case and where its outcome stops being public.

transition_in.introduces: What integrating it cost.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The engineering blog documents consolidation at four layers, each followed past 2023 to its last documented state, so some evidence is dated 2024.

transition_in.introduces: The layers the engineering blog does document.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Infrastructure and cloud were consolidated: EU5 onto AWS, SCHIP onto EKS at 2,000+ nodes across 25 marketplaces, and 732 AWS accounts and 425 Google Cloud projects mapped to teams and cost centers.

evidence.what: 'to a single public cloud vendor' (AWS), Canada to Google Cloud; 30+ clusters (2023), 'over 2,000 Kubernetes nodes' in 30 clusters 'across 25 marketplaces' (2024); 732 AWS accounts, 425 Google Cloud projects (Dec 2024), fewer than 150 in 2019.
evidence.shows: Shows the infrastructure layer consolidated and governed per team.

transition_in.introduces: The first: infrastructure and cloud.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Data ran on a central event platform while Adevinta Spain built a data mesh whose contracts cut the time to usable data from about five days to about 30 minutes.

evidence.what: Nearly a billion events a day over Kafka (2022); Databricks lakehouse with data mesh principles and immutable data contracts (2024).
evidence.shows: Shows a shared data substrate with domain-owned products.

transition_in.introduces: The data layer.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Chat and moderation were consolidated without a published architecture, while several narrower shared services are documented with their scale.

evidence.what: Shared services: Text in Image OCR, image models, YAMS media, dispute back office, Houston experimentation, each with scale and date.
evidence.shows: Shows uniform, high-volume services shared across marketplaces.

transition_in.introduces: The overarching components.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The dispute back office is the only cross-marketplace product component with a published architecture, built to normalize each marketplace's events into a common model.

evidence.what: Kafka, SQS or REST events normalized behind a Kotlin API, extensible micro-frontend; 'We couldn't hardcode anything… or make any assumptions.'
evidence.shows: Shows what a shared product component had to do to fit many marketplaces.

evidence.what: Figure 3 and an INFERENCE, NOT DOCUMENTED callout: per-tenant ingestion, canonical model, extensible front end; the component is only as good as the worst tenant's events.
evidence.shows: Shows, labeled as inference, why product components move integration work into event contracts.

transition_in.carries_over: The narrow shared services in the table, among them the dispute back office.
transition_in.introduces: The one product component with a published design.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Experimentation is the best-documented consolidation: ten A/B tools in 22 marketplaces became one platform through a build-buy-bridge decision, around a statistics package harvested from Marktplaats.

evidence.what: Houston chosen over buy with a third-party bridge; 2023 benchmark of 21 companies; Fisher used in more than 90% of Marktplaats experiments within a year, then group-wide.
evidence.shows: Shows a shared capability grown from a local one by a recorded decision.

transition_in.carries_over: The documented shared services and the one product component.
transition_in.introduces: The consolidation documented end to end: experimentation.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Machine learning followed the same path, with the 2024 ML Golden Path replacing scattered tooling with one workflow and a catalog that accepts promoted components.

evidence.what: 'a set of scattered tooling' replaced by one workflow on SCHIP and a central catalog (August 2024).
evidence.shows: Shows the same consolidate-and-harvest shape at the ML layer.

transition_in.introduces: The same path for machine learning.

sections.heading: Phase 4: Verticals and the Convergence Bet (2023 to Mid-2024)

flow.rationale: The strategy and revenue mix set the context; then the decision, its last progress report, the author's reading of it and what the rationale actually supports; last, the capability the rationale names first. The reading must follow the documented decision so it is not mistaken for it.

sections.heading: Phase 5: Decentralization and Break-Up (Mid-2024 to 2026)
sections.controlling_idea: Under its new owners Adevinta decentralized to standalone marketplaces, and the strategic reports show what unwinding a shared platform cost.

advances_thesis.how: Documents the reversal and its costs, and gives the author's reading of why it happened.

flow.rationale: The stated move, how it was organized, what it cost, what was left, and then why: the reading comes last so it rests on the documented costs.

transition_in.carries_over: The convergence last reported in May 2024.
transition_in.introduces: What the new owners did from July 2024.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: In July 2024, two months after the take-private settled, Adevinta started a new operating model, which the 2025 report describes as a move from a centralized structure to standalone marketplaces.

evidence.what: "The Group has evolved from a centralised structure to a decentralised, standalone operating model... ramp-down of central functions, the transfer of key capabilities, the localisation of intellectual property..."
evidence.shows: States the reversal in the company's words.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The group carried out the move knowing its risks: it created standalone local teams while its own 2024 risk register named operational and data decentralization as risks.

evidence.what: 'standalone teams across core functions to strengthen local market ownership'; 'operational decentralisation (which may affect areas such as… trust and fraud) and data decentralisation'.
evidence.shows: Shows the reversal was organized and its risks foreseen.

transition_in.introduces: How it was organized and what risks were named.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The strategic reports, not the engineering posts, show what decentralizing a shared platform cost: central and local services run in parallel, intellectual property localized in new legal entities, a carve-out with advisors, a smaller group and infrastructure owned by the marketplaces.

evidence.what: Parallel running (cloud emissions 'more than doubled'); IP localized and a Spanish branch for Kleinanzeigen.de GmbH (3 March 2026); a carve-out with EY; Spain sold 27 February 2026 with a gain of about €1.1 billion; headcount 4,439; leboncoin's own infrastructure team.
evidence.source: Strategic Report 2025; EQT 2025; Adevinta Tech Blog 2026; leboncoin tech blog 2026
evidence.shows: Shows each kind of cost decentralization carried.

transition_in.introduces: What carrying it out cost.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The 2025 accounts show a smaller group of six remaining businesses with €1,891 million of revenue from continuing operations.

evidence.what: Revenue €1,891 million; adjusted EBITDA €865 million (€970 million including Spain); portfolio as of October 2026.
evidence.shows: Shows the group the reversal left.

transition_in.introduces: The group that remained.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: My reading is that the reversal was economic before it was technical: a shared platform that was a synergy asset becomes a separation cost when value is realized by selling marketplaces, so platform topology must match the capital strategy.

evidence.what: Figure 5: the same shared platform as synergy asset and as separation cost.
evidence.shows: Shows the same topology priced two ways.

transition_in.introduces: Why the economics flipped.

sections.heading: Trade-offs the Case Illustrates
sections.controlling_idea: The right line between shared and local depends on the layer, on how uniform the technology is, and on how long the group expects to own each tenant.

advances_thesis.how: Compares the five sharing options the record shows.

transition_in.introduces: The options a group chooses between, with the ownership horizon as a condition.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Once separability can be built in, the question is when to share at all, and the right line between shared and local depends on the layer, on how uniform the technology is, and on how long the group expects to own each tenant, the last condition being the one the record adds to the 2019 test.

evidence.what: Five options: share infrastructure, narrow services, product components, converge product platforms, decentralize; what the record shows, when each is right and when it fails.
evidence.shows: Shows the options side by side, not as a maturity ladder.

sections.heading: The Chief Architect's View
sections.controlling_idea: Adevinta's record gives five decision rules: share by layer, grow by adoption, fund convergence separately, design for separability and expect owners to reverse strategy.

advances_thesis.how: Turns the record into the author's labeled rules.

transition_in.carries_over: What the record shows and where it stops.
transition_in.introduces: The rules the author takes from it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Of the five decision rules Adevinta's record gives, the first is to decide what to share by layer, writing the 2019 two-part test into the group's architecture principles.
Grow platforms by adoption and harvest local inventions, measuring a platform by how many tenants choose it.

transition_in.carries_over: The first rule, the layer test.
transition_in.introduces: The second rule, from the documented successes.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Treat product-platform convergence as its own investment case, with scope, stage gates and a plan that survives a change of owner.

transition_in.introduces: The third rule, for convergence.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Make separability a design requirement reviewed like security, asking of each shared capability what a departing tenant takes, what is switched off and what runs twice.

evidence.what: Figure 6: separability designed in through four connectors.
evidence.shows: Shows the four properties that let a tenant leave.

transition_in.introduces: The fourth rule, for owners who may sell.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Expect owners to reverse platform strategy within a year, and keep the platform cheap to reshape in either direction.

transition_in.introduces: The fifth rule.

flow.rationale: The layer test comes first because the other four rules apply it: adoption is how layers that pass it grow, convergence is the case that fails it, separability and owner reversals are what the ownership horizon adds. conclusion.heading: From Adevinta to OLX
conclusion.synthesis: Asked of every phase, the opening's three questions add up to one rule: what was shared held where the 2019 test said it would (uniform, expensive layers grown by adoption); the layer mattered most when the line moved up to the product platform, which fails the uniform-technology test and is never shown finished; and the cost was set by the owner, not the architecture, since the same layers were synergy in 2021 and separation in 2025. So: share by layer, fund product convergence as its own case, and design each shared layer for a tenant's exit.
conclusion.so_what: A Chief Architect can apply the rule from the public record alone, without knowing how Adevinta's convergence ended: share by layer, fund product convergence as its own case with scope and stage gates, and size every shared layer for the day a tenant leaves.

callback.to: The hook: Adevinta ran the whole centralization pendulum and wrote much of it down.
callback.how: The reader can now say what each swing of the pendulum shared, at which layer and at what cost, and why the last swing's outcome is unknown.

takeaway.content: Put the two-part test and the separability question to every shared capability; read case-olx next for what happens when the portfolio changes on its own, not together with the platform strategy.
